newsitem.title: RUSSIA: ALBRIGHT PLANS SECOND MOSCOW SESSION WITH PRIMAKOV.
newsitem.headline: ALBRIGHT PLANS SECOND MOSCOW SESSION WITH PRIMAKOV.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright prepared on Friday for a second meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov to try to narrow gaps over NATO's planned eastward expansion, U.S. officials said.

The previously unscheduled meeting was slotted in before Albright was due to return to Washington after a 24-hour visit to Moscow to push forward talks on a NATO-Russia security charter designed to calm Russian fears over alliance enlargement.

Albright and Primakov held two hours of talks on Thursday and said later they had made progress but that tough issues remained to be resolved if a May 27 target date for signing the charter was to be met.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, who leads the charter negotiations for the alliance, is to see Primakov in Luxembourg on May 6.
Western officials say the charter would set up a joint council with the Russians which would give Moscow a voice in key decisions affecting its security interests in Europe.

But Russia is demanding binding guarantees from the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation that it will not move nuclear weapons or conventional forces into the territory of the new members, whose names will be announced at a July summit in Madrid. NATO says it has no plans to do so, but is reluctant to be tied down legally.

Also holding up the charter negotiations is the failure of 30-nation Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) talks in Vienna so far to agree on new force levels on Russia's borders in the new post-Cold War era.

Earlier on Friday, Albright told an audience of Russian intellectuals and academics that NATO expansion would be in Russia's interests, and painted a disastrous scenario of what would happen if it did not take place.

The prospect of joining NATO was already forcing East European countries to resolve old ethnic and border disputes, and their membership would give them confidence to pursue arms control and build closer ties with Russia, she said.
"It is precisely because NATO is taking in new members that we can now avert the threat of of a major military build-up in central Europe," Albright said at the Carnegie Centre.

But if NATO did not enlarge, old dividing lines would re- emerge, confidence would disintegrate in Eastern Europe "and a new destabilising scramble for security would result," causing relations to crumble between Russia and its neighbours.

Albright said NATO's CFE proposals would ensure that each sate maintained only the military capabilities needed for its legitimate security needs, "so no NATO member, old or new, can become a staging ground for potential attack against Russia." REUTER
